1.pericope_label: The fifth trumpet: the fallen star, the opened pit, and the locusts

schools.summary: Take the star for a good angel of the invisible world, the falling meaning only swiftness; make the locusts the Persians and supply a sixth-century chronology of Jewish suffering to match; or else take them for military hordes best answering to the Saracens, with the scorpions as archers — and report, with impatience, the rival identifications of the angel with Satan, with Mohammed and even with the German reformer.

Argue from the perfect participle that the star was already fallen, and from the parallels of Lucifer and the lightning that a great evil power is meant, so that a good angel is hardly possible; distinguish this darkening, which hinders the light from outside, from the earlier one, which enfeebled the luminaries themselves; and keep the locusts to the Egyptian plague and to Joel, armed here with the sting of scorpions.

Report the identification of the star with an eminent bishop and with Boniface the third, who took the title of universal bishop from a usurping emperor as the reward of flattery and so became the devil’s turnkey.

Apply the whole to the eastern antichrist and the publishing of the Alcoran, and rule the literal insects out on the ground that these spare the grass and have a king, along with devils and the Gothic invaders.

Read the star as the old enemy opening the hearts of his own by blasphemous doctrine, the smoke as the madness of heresy that darkens even the lofty, and the locusts as members of the dragon’s body cleaving to one another.

debates: Whether the fallen star is a good angel (Wesley) or an evil power, which Ellicott argues from the grammar and the parallels and Robertson from the tense.
Whom the star and the locusts stand for — a Roman bishop (Henry), Mahomet (Gill), the Saracens or the Romans (Clarke), the Persians (Wesley), or the leaders of heresy (Bede).
What kind of darkening the smoke causes, which Ellicott alone distinguishes from the darkening of the previous trumpet.
Whether the locusts are natural, diabolical, or human, and how the sting of scorpions modifies the figure drawn from the Egyptian plague.
outliers: Wesley alone makes the opener of the pit a holy angel, against everyone else.
Ellicott alone contrasts the mechanism of this obscuration with that of the preceding vision.
Clarke alone lists the rival identifications of the angel and lets one of them stand as an absurdity.
Wesley alone dates the affliction to particular years and names the president who was put to death.

4.pericope_label: The locusts restrained: vegetation spared, the sealed exempt, five months of torment

schools.summary: Note that the command is given impersonally and might come from the king of the pit rather than from God; argue that locusts which spare vegetation and cannot touch the sealed are not literal, and that the promise of Luke 10:19, given just after the saying about Satan falling as lightning, guards against real injury but not against pain or death; take the five months for the natural span of the insect and so for a short period; and observe that the sufferers seek death without laying hands on themselves.

Read the spared grass and trees either as the low, middling and high degrees of men or as the prudent care of a general for his own supplies; identify the unsealed as the unbelieving Israelites, or as all false and heterodox Christians; and take the five months either literally, of the siege year, or prophetically at a day for a year, yielding a hundred and fifty.

Take the ban on killing as a limit on conquest rather than duration: the Saracens ravaged the eastern empire without destroying it or taking Constantinople, and the western locusts, the monks and friars, kill souls but not bodies.

debates: Who issues the command that restrains the locusts, which Barnes declines to settle.
Whether the spared vegetation is a figure for ranks of men or a note of military prudence.
Who the unsealed are — the heterodox, the unbelieving Israelites, or those merely reckoned outside.
Whether the five months are the natural term of a locust plague, the months of a particular siege, or a hundred and fifty years by the day-for-a-year rule.
outliers: Ellicott alone notices that the promise of Luke 10:19 follows the saying about Satan falling as lightning just as the safety of the sealed follows the fallen star here.
Clarke alone suspects the scorpion of the text is the artillery weapon of that name and cites Isidore and Seneca for it.
Barnes alone infers something about the sufferers from their not taking their own lives.
Robertson alone sets the longing for death here against Paul's desire to depart and be with Christ.
Gill alone measures the restraint by what the Saracens failed to capture.

7.pericope_label: The look of the locusts: horses, crowns, human faces, long hair, iron breastplates

schools.summary: Collect the travellers who compared the locust to a horse, then either doubt whether any of this description refers to the anatomy of the insect at all and dismiss the alleged human resemblance of its face with a parenthesis, or report that a commentator does see the resemblance; deny on the grammar that the long hair carries any note of sex, the faces being human rather than male; and trace the teeth, breastplates and chariot-noise to Joel.

Read the vision as an overwhelming military force, whether the troops of Mohammed, whose Arabs ride as though horse and man were one animal, or the Persians, a people neither wholly civilised nor wholly savage; take the crowns for turbans and for the extent of the conquests, and the human faces to mean that the locusts are really men.

Identify the hair with the Saracens on Pliny's report that the Arabians wore it long and were attired as women, derive Hagarene from Hagar and Saracen from Sarah, and turn the same figure against the monks and friars, whose iron breastplate is a seared conscience and the protection of princes, worn against the truth rather than for it.

debates: Whether the details of the vision describe the anatomy of a real locust at all, which Ellicott doubts and Barnes and Robertson pursue.
Whether the long hair marks effeminacy, as Barnes and Gill take it, or mere length, as Robertson argues from the word for men.
Whom the armed horsemen represent — the troops of Mohammed, the Romans, the Persians, the Saracens, or the religious orders of the West.
Whether the crowns are literal turbans or a figure for the extent of the conquests.
outliers: Ellicott alone refuses the anatomical method as a whole and marks the word distant as most needful.
Robertson alone reports a commentator who claims to see the human face in the locust.
Robertson alone rules the question of sex out of the long hair on the ground that the text says men generically and not males.
Barnes alone cites a witness while noting that the witness had no intention of confirming Scripture.
Gill alone derives the names Hagarene and Saracen and offers rival etymologies for the second.

10.pericope_label: The sting in the tail, the king of the abyss named Abaddon, and the first woe past

schools.summary: Locate the power deliberately in the tails and note the range of the word for sting; deny that the natural locust has any sting at all and distinguish doing wrong from tormenting; rule out the search for anatomical counterparts as vain, since these visions cannot be pictorially realised without grotesque incongruity; fix on the proverb that the locust has no king to show the movement is directed by a hidden spiritual force; and either refuse to seek a historical personage or weigh Abaddon against Death, Satan and a doubtful allusion to Apollo.

Read the tail as the false prophet and the sting as pernicious doctrine; apply the day-for-a-year rule to the five months, reaching a hundred and fifty years or seventy-nine; report that the king is thought to be Mohammed or Vespasian, or distinguish Abaddon from the dragon whose proper name is Satan; and date the end of the first woe to 589 and the rise of the papacy to Phocas in 606.

Make the sting the doctrine of Mahomet and of the Romish clergy, who set decrees and unwritten traditions above the word of God, and identify the king as Mahomet over the eastern locusts and the pope over the western.

debates: Whether the locusts of the vision have any counterpart in the natural insect, which Ellicott denies as a matter of method.
Whether the five prophetic months yield a hundred and fifty years or seventy-nine, two answers from the same day-for-a-year rule.
Who the king of the abyss is — an evil angel, Death, Satan, Mohammed, Vespasian, or no historical person at all.
Whether the hurt inflicted is bodily torment or the distress of wrong done, which Barnes argues from the change of verb.
outliers: Barnes alone denies the locust any sting and explains the ovipositor that has been mistaken for one.
Robertson alone remarks that the power to hurt might have been placed in other organs than the tails.
Ellicott alone lays down a general rule that these visions cannot be pictorially realised.
Robertson alone reports the conjecture that Apollyon alludes to Apollo, and rejects it.
Wesley alone distinguishes Abaddon from Satan as a different person under a different name.

13.pericope_label: The sixth trumpet: the voice from the golden altar and the four angels loosed at the Euphrates

schools.summary: Reconstruct the golden altar of incense and its ornamental horns and note that the order issues from the place of offering; decline to insist that literal angels are meant or that the number four counts divisions; supply the geography of the Euphrates as the eastern boundary of the empire; and either take the hour, day, month and year as the duration of the plague or deny that reading outright, arguing that the angels are made ready unto an appointed moment rather than for a length of time.

Take the voice from the altar of incense to mean that the wrath shall be delayed by no further intercession; reason that the bound angels must be evil, since good ones would not be bound; and either resolve the four measures of time into two hundred and twelve years matched to the caliphs Ali, Abubeker, Omar and Osman, or set out the same components and decline the calculation as an uncertainty not worth discussing.

Observe that the enemies of the church are restrained until God gives the word, that his instruments may lie far from those they will punish, and that prophetic characters of time are hardly to be understood by us.
Identify the loosed angels with the Turks, whose passage of the river and founding of their empire is dated to about 1301.

debates: Whether the four bound angels are evil spirits, agents of God's wrath, or a figure for human armies.
Whether the hour, day, month and year measure how long the plague lasts or fix the moment at which it begins.
Whether the four measures may be resolved into a definite number of years, which Wesley does and Clarke expressly declines to do.
What the voice from the horns of the golden altar signifies, and whether the mention dates the book while the temple still stood.
outliers: Wesley alone infers the moral character of the angels from the fact that they were bound.
Clarke alone lays out the arithmetic of the prophetic periods and then refuses to perform it.
Ellicott alone rejects the duration reading on the force of the preposition and reads the phrase as an appointed hour.
Clarke alone treats the golden altar as evidence for the date of the book.
Wesley alone matches the number of the angels to the number of the first caliphs.

16.pericope_label: Two hundred million horsemen, the breastplates of three colours, and the fire from their mouths

schools.summary: Convert the two myriads of myriads to two hundred millions while denying it can be literal, and hear in it an echo of the chariots of God in the Psalm; divide over the colour of jacinth, whether deep purple, the dark hue of smoke, or a red bordering on black, and note that the Greek makes the three adjectives metaphors without any particle of comparison; observe that power in the tail is natural for a scorpion but not a horse, and that the plague now works by mouth and tail together where the previous one worked by tail alone.

Grant the arithmetic but doubt the literal host, which could find no forage on earth, and mock the interpreters who make the number cover every soldier of the whole war; then ask whether the fire, smoke and brimstone are an allegory of gunpowder and the lion-headed horses of cannon, ornamented at muzzle and breech, such as the Ottomans used against the Greek empire.

Take the number as proof that the angels were men and find the Turks in it, whose strength was cavalry and whose ensign is a horse's tail; treat the guns as settled fact rather than conjecture, since Constantinople fell to them; and note the versions that read by these three plagues, and that the third part here is the eastern empire as it was the western before.

debates: Whether the two hundred millions are a countable army, an immense host beyond numbering, or a figure whose very size forbids a literal fulfilment.
What colour jacinth names, on which the four expositors give four answers.
Whether the fire, smoke and brimstone from the horses' mouths allegorise artillery and gunpowder — a question for Clarke and a settled fact for Gill.
Whether the vision points to a particular conquest or teaches only that worldliness provokes its own retribution.
outliers: Clarke alone objects that so vast an army could find no forage anywhere on earth.
Clarke alone answers a rival interpretation by quoting the Lord's words about receiving a hard saying.
Robertson alone points out that the Greek supplies no word of comparison, so that the three colours are metaphors outright.
Ellicott alone quotes a living poet to fix the colour of smoke.
Barnes alone remarks that we speak of power in the tail of a fish or a wasp but never of a horse.

20.pericope_label: The rest of men repented not: idols, murders, sorceries, and the limits of interpretation

schools.summary: Insist that a judgment which destroys a third and reforms nobody is the point of the passage, and defer the exposition until the reference of the whole trumpet is settled; trace the enumeration of idols by material to Daniel and the taunt of their helplessness to the psalms, note that the word for sorcery meant enchantment before it meant drug, and build the case for the Turkish power out of Gibbon and the reckoning by myriads — while conceding that the same likeness of language would be expected if the book had been written after the event.

Take the unpunished remainder for the western antichristian party, spared by the Turks and unreformed, and read the unrepented murders as the persecutions of the Waldenses and Albigenses, of Huss and Jerome of Prague, of the Marian martyrs and the victims of the Paris and Irish massacres, with the Inquisition continuing still.

Apply every vice in the list to Rome — sorceries as bleeding images and miracles pretended at tombs and wells, fornication as honour given to creatures, thefts as the price of indulgences — and then deny that this is certainly the true interpretation, observing that among some to doubt it is little short of heresy.

debates: Why so great a judgment produces no repentance, and what that failure is meant to teach.
Whether the idolatry censured is pagan image-worship or the practice of the western church.
Whether the vices of the last verse may be identified item by item with abuses of Rome, which Clarke sets out in full and then refuses to affirm.
Whether the Turkish conquest is the fulfilment of the sixth trumpet, and how far a resemblance of language can establish it.
outliers: Clarke alone completes a partisan exposition and then withdraws his assent to it, rebuking those who treat doubt as heresy.
Barnes alone notices that the very likeness between the vision and the historian would be expected if the book had been written after the events.
Barnes alone postpones the meaning of the passage until the reference of the whole trumpet has been argued.
Robertson alone suggests that the hideousness of idol faces may follow from their being reckoned as demons.
Robertson alone follows the word for sorcery down to the modern trade in patent medicines.
